questions.q: What is the pretraining objective used by decoder-only LLMs such as GPT and Llama?
options: Predicting randomly masked tokens using context on both sides
Reconstructing corrupted spans of text with a separate decoder
Predicting the next token given all previous tokens
Classifying whether two sentences are consecutive
questions.why: Decoder-only models are trained with causal (autoregressive) language modeling: each position predicts the next token while attending only to earlier tokens. Masked-token prediction with bidirectional context is the BERT-style objective, which does not directly train a model to generate text left to right.

questions.q: A team is pretraining an encoder-only model like BERT for classification and retrieval tasks. Which objective is the standard choice?
options: Causal language modeling
Span corruption with sentinel tokens
Masked language modeling
Contrastive image-text alignment
questions.why: BERT-style encoders hide a fraction of input tokens (about 15% in the original paper) and learn to predict them using context from both directions. Causal LM is the decoder-only objective; it gives only left context and is not how BERT was trained.

questions.q: Which model family popularized the *span corruption* pretraining objective, where contiguous spans are replaced by sentinel tokens and the decoder reconstructs them?
options: T5 (encoder-decoder)
GPT (decoder-only)
BERT (encoder-only)
CLIP (dual encoder)
questions.why: T5 masks contiguous spans, replaces each with a unique sentinel token, and trains the decoder to output the missing spans. BERT masks individual tokens and predicts them in place without a generative decoder, so it is a related but different objective.

questions.q: What is the main outcome of the pretraining stage of an LLM?
options: A model that reliably follows user instructions and refuses unsafe requests
A model specialized for one downstream task
A compact model distilled from a larger teacher
A base model with broad language knowledge learned from a large unlabeled corpus
questions.why: Pretraining on trillions of tokens of self-supervised text produces a general-purpose base (foundation) model. Instruction following and refusal behavior come later, from SFT and alignment; a raw base model typically just continues text.

questions.q: Why do LLM pretraining pipelines remove duplicate and near-duplicate documents?
options: To increase the vocabulary size of the tokenizer
To make every document the same length
To guarantee the model never sees copyrighted text
To reduce memorization and wasted compute on repeated content
questions.why: Duplicated text skews the data distribution, wastes training tokens and increases verbatim memorization (and regurgitation). Deduplication does not by itself address licensing or copyright; that requires separate source filtering.

questions.q: A data engineer needs GPU-accelerated tools to deduplicate, filter and clean a multi-terabyte web corpus before pretraining. Which NVIDIA tool is designed for this?
options: NeMo Curator
NeMo Guardrails
TensorRT-LLM
Triton Inference Server
questions.why: NeMo Curator provides scalable data-curation modules (text extraction, language identification, heuristic and classifier quality filtering, exact/fuzzy deduplication) that can use GPUs through RAPIDS. NeMo Guardrails controls runtime conversations of a deployed model and plays no role in preparing training data.

questions.q: During corpus curation, a pipeline drops documents with very high symbol-to-word ratios, excessive repeated lines, or very short length. What kind of step is this?
options: Heuristic quality filtering
Fuzzy deduplication
Tokenization
Benchmark decontamination
questions.why: Rule-based heuristics (length, punctuation and symbol ratios, repetition, stop-word presence) cheaply remove boilerplate and low-quality text. Fuzzy deduplication instead compares documents to each other to find near-copies, regardless of their quality.

questions.q: A company has 50 GB of unlabeled internal engineering documents and wants a base model to absorb the domain's vocabulary and facts. Which approach fits best?
options: Prompt tuning with 20 virtual tokens
Direct Preference Optimization
Continued (domain-adaptive) pretraining
Instruction tuning on a public chat dataset
questions.why: Continued pretraining keeps the same next-token objective on a large unlabeled domain corpus, letting the model learn domain language and knowledge. DPO and instruction tuning need labeled preference pairs or prompt-response pairs and teach behavior rather than bulk domain knowledge.

questions.q: What does a typical supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset for a chat model consist of?
options: Prompt and target-response pairs written or curated as demonstrations
Pairs of chosen and rejected responses for the same prompt
Raw web documents with no labels
Scalar reward scores for each generated token
questions.why: SFT trains the model with ordinary cross-entropy to imitate demonstration responses for given prompts. Chosen/rejected pairs are preference data used for reward modeling or DPO, a later alignment stage.

questions.q: Instruction tuning (e.g., FLAN-style training on many tasks phrased as instructions) primarily aims to:
options: Increase the model's maximum context length
Compress the model for faster inference
Improve zero-shot generalization to new instructions not seen in training
Teach the model a new tokenizer
questions.why: Training on a diverse mix of tasks expressed as natural-language instructions teaches the model to follow instructions in general, so it handles unseen tasks better zero-shot. It does not change architecture-level properties like context length or model size.

questions.q: What distinguishes parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) from full fine-tuning?
options: PEFT trains on fewer examples but updates all weights
PEFT freezes most pretrained weights and trains a small number of added or selected parameters
PEFT uses only reinforcement learning instead of supervised loss
PEFT requires removing transformer layers from the model
questions.why: Methods such as LoRA, adapters and prompt tuning typically train well under 1–2% of the parameters, cutting gradient and optimizer-state memory. PEFT is about which parameters are trained, not the dataset size; it can use just as much data as full fine-tuning.

questions.q: How does LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapt a frozen weight matrix W?
options: It prunes W to a lower rank and fine-tunes the remainder
It learns an update ΔW = B·A, where B and A are small low-rank matrices, and adds it to W
It prepends trainable vectors to the input sequence
It quantizes W to 4 bits and trains the quantized values
questions.why: LoRA keeps W frozen and trains a low-rank factorization of the weight update, so for a d×k matrix only r·(d+k) parameters are trained. Prepending trainable vectors to the input describes prompt tuning, a different PEFT method.

questions.q: In a LoRA configuration, what does the rank `r` control?
options: The number of transformer layers that are fine-tuned
The number of bits used to store the base weights
The inner dimension of the low-rank matrices, and thus adapter capacity and size
The number of attention heads per layer
questions.why: A has shape r×k and B has shape d×r, so r sets how expressive the update can be and how many parameters are trained; common values are 4–64. The set of layers adapted is controlled separately by `target_modules`, not by r.

questions.q: In standard LoRA, A is randomly initialized and B is initialized to zeros. What is the consequence at the start of training?
options: Training cannot begin until B is warmed up with a separate loss
The adapter immediately adds random noise to the model output
The adapted model initially behaves exactly like the base model because ΔW = 0
Gradients for A are always zero throughout training
questions.why: With B = 0, the product B·A is zero, so fine-tuning starts from the pretrained function and drifts away smoothly. A's gradient is zero only at the very first step (it depends on B); once B is updated, A receives gradients too.

questions.q: After LoRA fine-tuning, an engineer merges the adapter into the base weights (W' = W + B·A). What is the main benefit for deployment?
options: No extra inference latency, because the model has the original architecture and size
The model becomes smaller than the original base model
The adapter can still be hot-swapped per request
The model automatically supports a longer context window
questions.why: Merging folds the low-rank update into each target matrix, so inference runs the same dense matmuls as the base model with no adapter overhead. The trade-off is that the adapter can no longer be swapped dynamically; keeping it separate is what enables per-request adapter switching.

questions.q: What is QLoRA?
options: Training a model from scratch entirely in 4-bit integers
Post-training quantization of a LoRA adapter for faster serving
A method that quantizes activations to FP8 during pretraining
LoRA fine-tuning on top of a frozen base model quantized to 4 bits
questions.why: QLoRA stores the frozen base weights in 4-bit NF4, dequantizes them on the fly for computation, and backpropagates into higher-precision LoRA adapters. This let a 65B model be fine-tuned on a single 48 GB GPU. It is a fine-tuning memory technique, not low-precision pretraining from scratch.

questions.q: Why does QLoRA use the 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) data type for the base weights?
options: It is natively supported by tensor cores for 4-bit matmuls
Its quantization levels are placed to suit normally distributed weights, giving lower error than uniform INT4
It stores weights with an 8-bit exponent like BF16
It removes the need for any dequantization during the forward pass
questions.why: Pretrained weights are roughly zero-centered and normally distributed, so NF4 places its 16 levels at quantiles of a normal distribution, making it information-theoretically well suited to them. NF4 is a storage format: weights are dequantized to BF16 for the actual matmul.

questions.q: Classic adapter tuning (Houlsby et al.) inserts which of the following into each transformer block?
options: A learned soft prompt at the input layer only
Small bottleneck feed-forward layers (down-projection, nonlinearity, up-projection) with a residual connection
Extra attention heads with full-rank weights
A second copy of the full feed-forward network
questions.why: Adapters are small sequential modules added inside each block while the original weights stay frozen. Unlike LoRA, they cannot be merged into existing weights, so they add some inference latency.

questions.q: In prompt tuning (soft prompting), what is actually trained?
options: A small set of continuous "virtual token" embeddings prepended to the input
The natural-language wording of a hard prompt chosen by search
The final output projection layer
The tokenizer's vocabulary
questions.why: Prompt tuning learns embedding vectors that need not correspond to real words, while the whole model stays frozen. Searching over discrete natural-language wording is prompt engineering, which involves no gradient-based training.

questions.q: How does prefix tuning differ from basic prompt tuning?
options: Prefix tuning trains the full embedding matrix
Prefix tuning adds trainable key/value prefix vectors at every transformer layer, not just at the input
Prefix tuning only works with encoder-only models
Prefix tuning uses discrete tokens selected from the vocabulary
questions.why: Prefix tuning injects learned prefix activations into the attention of every layer, giving more capacity than prompt tuning, which only adds embeddings at the input. Both keep the base weights frozen and use continuous, not discrete, vectors.

questions.q: What feature characterizes p-tuning, a method supported in NVIDIA NeMo?
options: It updates all attention weights with a low learning rate
It inserts adapters only into the final layer
It generates the virtual-token embeddings with a small trainable prompt encoder (e.g., an LSTM or MLP)
It replaces the model's tokenizer with a domain-specific one
questions.why: P-tuning reparameterizes soft prompts through a prompt encoder, which stabilizes optimization compared with learning the embeddings directly. After training, the encoder's outputs can be cached as fixed virtual tokens, so the base model stays frozen throughout.

questions.q: After fine-tuning on a narrow legal-contract dataset, a model performs worse on general reasoning and coding than before. What is this called?
options: Reward hacking
Exposure bias
Catastrophic forgetting
Mode collapse
questions.why: Updating weights on a narrow distribution can overwrite previously learned capabilities, degrading performance on tasks outside the fine-tuning data. Reward hacking is a reinforcement-learning failure in which the policy exploits a flawed reward, which is not involved in plain fine-tuning.

questions.q: What is the usual order of stages in the classic RLHF pipeline (as in InstructGPT)?
options: Train reward model → pretrain → SFT → PPO
SFT → train reward model on human preferences → optimize policy with PPO
PPO → SFT → train reward model
SFT → PPO → collect human preferences
questions.why: Starting from a pretrained model, SFT produces a reasonable policy, humans rank its outputs to train a reward model, and PPO then optimizes the policy against that reward. PPO cannot run before a reward model exists, because the reward model is what supplies its training signal.

questions.q: In RLHF, what does the reward model learn from and output?
options: It learns from raw web text and outputs next-token probabilities
It learns from SFT demonstrations and outputs a full response
It learns from human preference comparisons and outputs a scalar score for a prompt-response pair
It learns from benchmark accuracy and outputs a pass/fail label
questions.why: The reward model, usually an LM with a scalar head, is trained so preferred responses score higher than rejected ones. It is a judge of responses, not a generator; generating responses is the policy's job.

questions.q: In RLHF, what is PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) used for?
options: Training the reward model on preference pairs
Filtering low-quality data before pretraining
Updating the language model policy to maximize reward while limiting how far each update moves it
Merging LoRA adapters after fine-tuning
questions.why: PPO is the RL algorithm that adjusts the policy (the LLM) using rewards from the reward model, with a clipped objective that keeps each update small and stable. The reward model itself is trained by supervised pairwise loss, not by PPO.

questions.q: What is the key simplification that DPO offers compared with PPO-based RLHF?
options: It needs no preference data at all
It replaces SFT with unsupervised pretraining
It optimizes the policy directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, without a separate reward model or RL sampling loop
It trains only the reward model and leaves the policy unchanged
questions.why: DPO shows that the RLHF objective can be rewritten as a simple loss on chosen/rejected pairs, using a frozen reference model as an anchor. It still requires preference data; what it removes is the explicit reward model training and online PPO rollouts.

questions.q: Why does RLHF add a KL-divergence penalty between the policy and the reference (SFT) model?
options: To speed up tokenization during rollouts
To make the reward model more accurate
To reduce the number of GPUs needed
To stop the policy from drifting too far and exploiting reward-model weaknesses
questions.why: The KL term keeps generations close to the fluent SFT distribution, preventing reward hacking and degenerate text. It does not change the reward model itself; it regularizes the policy against over-optimizing that model's imperfect scores.

questions.q: In RLAIF, what replaces the human annotators of RLHF?
options: An AI model that produces the preference labels
A rule-based regex filter
The base model's perplexity score
Benchmark accuracy on held-out tests
questions.why: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback uses an LLM (often guided by written principles) to judge which response is better, making preference data cheap to scale. Perplexity measures how likely text is under a model, not which answer is more helpful or harmless, so it cannot serve as the preference labeler.

questions.q: What is the core idea of Constitutional AI-style alignment?
options: Hard-coding refusal rules into the tokenizer
Training only on government-approved datasets
Having the model critique and revise its own outputs against a written set of principles, then using AI feedback for preference training
Removing all safety training to maximize helpfulness
questions.why: The "constitution" is a list of natural-language principles; the model self-critiques and revises its responses for SFT, and an AI judge applies the principles to produce preference labels (RLAIF). The behavior is learned through training rather than enforced by fixed token-level rules.

questions.q: A team has only 200 labeled examples for a niche extraction task and wants a few thousand for fine-tuning. Which approach is most common?
options: Duplicate the 200 examples 20 times
Switch to masked language modeling
Use a strong LLM to generate additional examples, then filter them for quality
Train with a larger learning rate to compensate
questions.why: Synthetic data generation with a capable "teacher" model, followed by filtering (e.g., with a reward model or LLM judge), is a standard way to expand small datasets. Simple duplication adds no new information and mainly encourages overfitting.

questions.q: In knowledge distillation, what does the student model learn from?
options: Only the hard ground-truth labels
The teacher's gradients copied directly into its weights
A pruned copy of the teacher's attention heads
The teacher's output distributions (soft targets) or generated outputs
questions.why: Distillation trains a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher, typically by matching its softened probability distributions, which carry more information than one-hot labels. Pruning removes structure from a model; it is a separate compression technique, though it is often combined with distillation.

questions.q: What does mixed precision training mean?
options: Using different learning rates for different layers
Running most math in a 16-bit format while keeping numerically sensitive parts, such as master weights, in FP32
Mixing text and image data in the same batch
Storing weights in INT8 during training
questions.why: Mixed precision uses FP16 or BF16 for matmuls and activations to use Tensor Cores and save memory, while FP32 master weights and certain reductions preserve accuracy. Using different learning rates per layer is a separate optimization trick, unrelated to numeric precision.

questions.q: Why is loss scaling needed when training in FP16?
options: Small gradient values underflow to zero in FP16's limited exponent range
FP16 cannot represent negative numbers
FP16 matmuls are slower than FP32 without scaling
Loss values above 1.0 overflow in FP16
questions.why: Multiplying the loss by a scale factor shifts gradients into FP16's representable range during backprop; they are unscaled before the optimizer step. FP16's maximum is about 65,504, so a loss above 1.0 is no problem; the issue is tiny values, not moderate ones.

questions.q: Why is BF16 often preferred over FP16 for LLM training on A100/H100 GPUs?
options: BF16 has more mantissa bits, giving higher precision
BF16 uses half the memory of FP16
BF16 has the same 8-bit exponent range as FP32, so loss scaling is usually unnecessary
BF16 is the only format supported by Tensor Cores
questions.why: BF16 trades mantissa precision (7 bits versus FP16's 10) for FP32's dynamic range, which avoids underflow/overflow problems. Both are 16-bit formats with identical memory cost, and Tensor Cores support FP16 as well.

questions.q: Which NVIDIA library enables FP8 training of transformer layers on Hopper-class GPUs and is used by NeMo and Megatron-LM?
options: Transformer Engine
cuDF
TensorRT
DALI
questions.why: Transformer Engine provides FP8-aware transformer modules with automatic per-tensor scaling, using Hopper's FP8 Tensor Cores for training. TensorRT is an inference optimizer and does not run training loops.

questions.q: A model only fits a micro-batch of 2 per GPU, but the recipe calls for a larger batch. Which technique reaches the larger effective batch without more memory?
options: Gradient checkpointing
Gradient accumulation
Gradient clipping
Learning-rate warmup
questions.why: Gradient accumulation runs several forward/backward passes, sums their gradients, and only then takes one optimizer step, simulating a larger batch. Gradient checkpointing saves activation memory too, but it does not change the effective batch size.

questions.q: What trade-off does gradient (activation) checkpointing make?
options: Lower accuracy in exchange for faster training
More GPU memory in exchange for fewer communication steps
Less activation memory in exchange for recomputing activations during the backward pass
Smaller batch size in exchange for higher learning rate
questions.why: Only some activations (e.g., at layer boundaries) are stored; the rest are recomputed when needed for gradients, adding roughly one extra forward pass of compute. The results are mathematically the same, so model accuracy is not affected.

questions.q: Why do LLM training recipes start with a learning-rate warmup?
options: To let the tokenizer build its vocabulary
To reduce the final learning rate to zero
To allow a larger number of epochs
To avoid unstable, large updates early on, when weights and optimizer statistics are poorly estimated
questions.why: Early in training, Adam's moment estimates are noisy and gradients can be large, so ramping the LR up linearly over the first steps prevents divergence. Reducing the LR toward a minimum at the end is the job of the decay schedule, not warmup.

questions.q: After warmup, a training config specifies `scheduler: CosineAnnealing` with `min_lr: 1e-5`. What does this do?
options: Keeps the learning rate constant at the peak value
Cycles the learning rate between peak and zero every epoch
Increases the learning rate gradually until training ends
Smoothly decreases the learning rate from the peak toward 1e-5 following a cosine curve
questions.why: Cosine annealing decays the LR along half a cosine wave, decreasing slowly at first, faster in the middle and slowly near the end, and settles at the minimum. Cycling with restarts is a separate variant (SGDR); a plain cosine decay schedule decreases only once.

questions.q: What does `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)` protect against?
options: Vanishing gradients in deep networks
Exploding gradients causing excessively large updates
Overfitting on small datasets
Running out of GPU memory
questions.why: If the total gradient norm exceeds 1.0, all gradients are rescaled so the norm equals 1.0, bounding the step size and reducing loss spikes. Clipping only shrinks gradients, so it cannot help vanishing gradients, which are too small to begin with.

questions.q: In data parallelism, how is work divided across GPUs?
options: Each GPU holds a different subset of layers
Each GPU holds a slice of every weight matrix
Each GPU processes a different part of the sequence
Each GPU holds a full model replica and processes a different slice of the batch
questions.why: Every replica computes gradients on its own data shard, then gradients are averaged (all-reduce) so all copies stay identical. Splitting layers across GPUs is pipeline parallelism, which is used when a full replica does not fit on one GPU.

questions.q: Which parallelism strategy splits individual weight matrices (e.g., the columns of an MLP projection) across GPUs so each computes part of the same layer?
options: Tensor parallelism
Pipeline parallelism
Data parallelism
Expert parallelism
questions.why: Tensor (intra-layer) parallelism, as in Megatron-LM, shards matrices within each layer and exchanges partial results via collectives. Expert parallelism places whole MoE experts on different GPUs instead of splitting a single matrix.

questions.q: A model's 80 layers are split so GPU 0 runs layers 1–20, GPU 1 runs 21–40, and so on, with micro-batches flowing between stages. What is this?
options: Tensor parallelism
Pipeline parallelism
Sequence parallelism
ZeRO stage 1
questions.why: Pipeline (inter-layer) parallelism assigns consecutive layer groups to stages and streams micro-batches through them to keep stages busy. ZeRO stage 1 shards optimizer states across data-parallel ranks and does not split the model by layers.

questions.q: What do DeepSpeed ZeRO and PyTorch FSDP do to reduce memory in data-parallel training?
options: Shard optimizer states, gradients and/or parameters across data-parallel ranks instead of replicating them
Quantize weights to 4 bits during training
Recompute activations in the backward pass
Offload all computation to the CPU
questions.why: Plain data parallelism keeps a full copy of the weights, gradients and Adam states on every GPU; ZeRO/FSDP partition these and gather pieces only when needed. Activation recomputation is gradient checkpointing, a separate and complementary technique.

questions.q: What is NCCL's role in multi-GPU training?
options: It compiles models into optimized inference engines
It schedules jobs on a Kubernetes cluster
It stores model checkpoints on object storage
It provides optimized collective communication such as all-reduce and all-gather between GPUs
questions.why: The NVIDIA Collective Communications Library implements topology-aware collectives over NVLink, PCIe and InfiniBand, and is the default GPU backend for PyTorch distributed. Compiling inference engines is TensorRT's job, not NCCL's.

questions.q: An ML team wants an NVIDIA framework that covers pretraining, SFT, PEFT (LoRA, p-tuning) and alignment of LLMs at scale. Which should they choose?
options: NVIDIA Triton Inference Server
NVIDIA RAPIDS cuML
NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM
NVIDIA NeMo framework
questions.why: NeMo is NVIDIA's end-to-end framework for building and customizing generative AI models, with Megatron-based distributed training, PEFT recipes, and alignment tooling. TensorRT-LLM optimizes models for inference after training is complete.

questions.q: What is Megatron-LM (and its Megatron-Core library) best known for?
options: Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines
Guardrails for chatbot safety
Efficient large-scale transformer training with tensor, pipeline and sequence parallelism
GPU-accelerated data frames for ETL
questions.why: Megatron-LM introduced practical intra-layer tensor parallelism and combines it with pipeline and data parallelism to train models with hundreds of billions of parameters; NeMo builds on Megatron-Core. GPU data frames are provided by RAPIDS cuDF, not Megatron.

questions.q: Which NVIDIA toolkit was built specifically for scalable model alignment methods such as RLHF with PPO, DPO and SteerLM?
options: NeMo-Aligner
NeMo Curator
NeMo Retriever
NeMo Guardrails
questions.why: NeMo-Aligner provides distributed implementations of reward-model training, PPO-based RLHF, DPO and SteerLM on top of NeMo/Megatron. NeMo Guardrails adds runtime rules around a deployed model and does not change its weights.

questions.q: During a 5-epoch SFT run, training loss keeps falling, but validation loss reaches its minimum at epoch 2 and rises afterward. What is happening?
options: The learning rate is too low
The model is underfitting
The dataset contains too few duplicates
The model is overfitting the fine-tuning data after epoch 2
questions.why: A widening gap between falling training loss and rising validation loss is the classic overfitting signature; using the epoch-2 checkpoint or early stopping is appropriate. Underfitting would show both losses staying high, not a falling training loss.

questions.q: A support bot must answer from product documentation that changes every week, and answers must cite sources. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Full fine-tuning every week
Continued pretraining on the documentation
Retrieval-augmented generation over the documentation
Prompt tuning with 100 virtual tokens
questions.why: RAG keeps knowledge in an updatable index and lets the model cite retrieved passages, without any retraining when documents change. Weekly fine-tuning is costly, risks forgetting, and gives no reliable way to trace answers to sources.

questions.q: Why do long training jobs save model checkpoints regularly?
options: To reduce GPU memory during the forward pass
To make the loss curve smoother
To allow resuming after failures and to select or evaluate intermediate models
To increase throughput by caching activations
questions.why: A training checkpoint saves weights plus optimizer and scheduler state so a job can restart after a node failure and so earlier versions can be evaluated or rolled back to. It is unrelated to activation memory; that is the "checkpointing" in gradient checkpointing, a different concept with a confusingly similar name.

questions.q: According to the Chinchilla scaling study, roughly how many training tokens per parameter are compute-optimal?
options: About 1 token per parameter
About 1,000 tokens per parameter
About 2 tokens per parameter
About 20 tokens per parameter
questions.why: Hoffmann et al. found that, for a fixed compute budget, parameters and tokens should scale together at about 20 tokens per parameter (e.g., 70B params with 1.4T tokens). Many modern models train far beyond this because inference cost favors smaller, longer-trained models, but 20 is the compute-optimal rule of thumb.

questions.q: LoRA with rank r = 8 is applied to one 4096 × 4096 projection matrix. How many trainable parameters does this adapter add?
questions.why: A is r × 4096 and B is 4096 × r, so the count is r·(d + k) = 8 × (4096 + 4096) = 65,536. 32,768 counts only one of the two matrices, and 16,777,216 is the size of the full frozen matrix.

questions.q: A 32-layer model with hidden size 4096 gets LoRA (r = 8) on `q_proj` and `v_proj` only, each 4096 × 4096. How many trainable parameters in total?
questions.why: Each adapted matrix has 8 × (4096 + 4096) = 65,536 parameters; 2 matrices × 32 layers × 65,536 = 4,194,304, about 0.06% of a 7B model. 2,097,152 forgets one of the two target modules, and 8,388,608 would correspond to r = 16.

questions.q: In standard LoRA the update is scaled by α/r. With `r=16` and `lora_alpha=32`, what is the scaling factor applied to B·A?
questions.why: The scaling is α/r = 32/16 = 2. A common heuristic sets α = 2r so the effective scale stays constant when r changes; 0.5 is the inverse ratio r/α, which is a frequent mix-up.

questions.q:
```python
config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"],
                    task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(base_model, config)
```

Which weights will be trained?
options: All attention and MLP weights in the base model
Only new low-rank matrices attached to the query and value projections
The query and value projection weights themselves, updated in full
Only the language-model head
questions.why: `get_peft_model` freezes the base model and injects LoRA A/B matrices into modules whose names match `q_proj` and `v_proj`. The original q/v weights stay frozen; only the added low-rank matrices receive gradients.

questions.q:
After wrapping a model with PEFT, `model.print_trainable_parameters()` prints:
`trainable params: 4,194,304 || all params: 6,742,609,920 || trainable%: 0.0622`
What does this tell the engineer?
options: The base model has been compressed to 4.2M parameters
The adapter will make inference about 0.06% slower
Only 6.7B parameters will be saved in the adapter checkpoint
Gradients and optimizer states are needed for only about 4.2M parameters
questions.why: Only trainable parameters need gradients and Adam states, which is where PEFT's memory savings come from; the adapter checkpoint is just these ~4.2M parameters (~8–17 MB). The base model still has all 6.7B parameters in memory for the forward pass; nothing is compressed.

questions.q: Training runs on 8 GPUs with data parallelism, a per-GPU micro-batch of 4, and `gradient_accumulation_steps=8`. What is the effective global batch size?
questions.why: Global batch = micro-batch × accumulation steps × data-parallel GPUs = 4 × 8 × 8 = 256 sequences per optimizer step. 32 counts only micro-batch × GPUs (or micro-batch × accumulation) and ignores the third factor.

questions.q: A pretraining run uses a global batch of 256 sequences of length 4,096 tokens. Approximately how many tokens are processed per optimizer step?
options: About 1.05 million
About 105 thousand
About 4.2 million
About 262 thousand
questions.why: 256 × 4,096 = 1,048,576 tokens per step, which is why LLM batch sizes are often quoted in tokens (here, ~1M). 4.2 million would require a sequence length of 16K or a global batch of 1,024.

questions.q: Using the rule of thumb of ~16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision training with Adam (excluding activations), roughly how much GPU memory does full fine-tuning of a 7B model need?
options: 14 GB
112 GB
28 GB
56 GB
questions.why: 7B × 16 bytes ≈ 112 GB for weights, gradients, FP32 master weights and two Adam moments, before activations, so it needs multiple GPUs or sharding. 14 GB is only the BF16 weights, enough for inference but not for training.

questions.q: Roughly how much memory do the frozen weights of a 7B-parameter base model occupy when stored in 4-bit NF4 for QLoRA (ignoring small quantization-constant overhead)?
options: About 3.5 GB
About 7 GB
About 14 GB
About 0.9 GB
questions.why: 4 bits is 0.5 bytes per parameter, so 7B × 0.5 B ≈ 3.5 GB, which is why QLoRA fits 7B fine-tuning on consumer GPUs. 7 GB would be 8-bit storage and 14 GB is BF16.

questions.q: Adam keeps two FP32 moment tensors (m and v) per trainable parameter. How much memory do these states alone take for full fine-tuning of a 7B model?
options: 28 GB
56 GB
14 GB
112 GB
questions.why: Two FP32 values = 8 bytes per parameter, so 7B × 8 B = 56 GB, often more than the weights themselves. 28 GB would count only one moment; this is exactly the memory that ZeRO stage 1 shards across GPUs.

questions.q: Which ZeRO stage partitions only the optimizer states across data-parallel ranks, while keeping full gradients and parameters on each GPU?
options: ZeRO stage 3
ZeRO-Offload
ZeRO stage 2
ZeRO stage 1
questions.why: Stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 additionally shards gradients, and stage 3 also shards the parameters. ZeRO-Offload moves states to CPU memory rather than describing a partitioning level.

questions.q: A team using ZeRO stage 1 still runs out of memory and wants the next stage without yet sharding parameters. What does ZeRO stage 2 add?
options: Partitioning of gradients in addition to optimizer states
Partitioning of model parameters
Pipeline-parallel scheduling
Automatic 4-bit quantization of weights
questions.why: Stage 2 shards gradients (reduce-scatter instead of all-reduce) on top of stage 1's optimizer-state sharding, with communication volume similar to standard data parallelism. Parameter sharding is the defining feature of stage 3.

questions.q: In PyTorch FSDP, which `ShardingStrategy` is broadly equivalent to ZeRO stage 3?
options: `NO_SHARD`
`SHARD_GRAD_OP`
`FULL_SHARD`
`DDP`
questions.why: `FULL_SHARD` shards parameters, gradients and optimizer states, gathering each unit's parameters just in time for forward and backward. `SHARD_GRAD_OP` shards only gradients and optimizer states, which corresponds to ZeRO stage 2.

questions.q: An engineer enables `model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()` to fit longer sequences. What change in training speed should they expect?
options: No change, because recomputation is free on Tensor Cores
Roughly 20–35% slower steps due to recomputing the forward pass during backward
About 2× faster due to lower memory traffic
About 4× slower because every layer is recomputed four times
questions.why: Full activation checkpointing adds about one extra forward pass; since the backward pass costs about twice the forward, the step costs roughly 4 units instead of 3 (~33% more). It is a memory-for-compute trade, so it never speeds training up.

questions.q: A fine-tuning run in FP16 on an A100 intermittently produces `loss = nan` and overflow warnings. What is the most effective fix?
options: Switch mixed precision from FP16 to BF16
Increase the learning rate
Disable gradient clipping
Increase LoRA rank
questions.why: BF16 has FP32's exponent range, so activations and gradients that overflow FP16's ~65,504 limit are representable, and A100 supports BF16 natively. Increasing the learning rate or removing clipping would make numerical instability worse.

questions.q: Midway through pretraining, the loss suddenly jumps from 2.1 to 7.5 and does not recover. What is a standard remediation?
options: Continue training and wait for it to recover by itself
Double the batch size immediately without restarting
Roll back to a checkpoint before the spike, skip the offending data batches, and possibly lower the LR
Switch the objective to masked language modeling
questions.why: Large-model training reports (e.g., PaLM, OPT) describe restarting from an earlier checkpoint and skipping the batches around a spike, often with a reduced learning rate. A spike that does not recover signals divergence; waiting typically just wastes compute.

questions.q: A new run diverges within the first 200 steps when starting directly at a peak LR of 3e-4. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Add a linear warmup over the first ~1–2k steps
Increase weight decay to 1.0
Remove the cosine decay at the end of training
Train for more epochs
questions.why: Starting at the peak LR with unstable early optimizer statistics often causes divergence; warmup ramps the LR gradually. Removing the end-of-training decay affects only late training and does nothing for instability in the first few hundred steps.

questions.q: Which learning-rate pairing is most typical when fine-tuning a 7B model?
options: Full fine-tuning ~1e-2; LoRA ~1e-6
Both use the pretraining peak LR of ~3e-4
Full fine-tuning ~1e-3; LoRA ~1e-7
Full fine-tuning ~1e-5; LoRA ~1e-4 to 2e-4
questions.why: Full fine-tuning uses small LRs to avoid destroying pretrained knowledge, while LoRA's freshly initialized, low-rank adapters usually need roughly 10× higher LRs. LRs like 1e-2 would quickly destabilize full fine-tuning of an LLM.

questions.q: After domain SFT, a model loses general instruction-following ability. Which data-side change best reduces this forgetting in the next run?
options: Remove the validation set to train on more data
Train for more epochs on the domain data only
Increase the learning rate
Mix a portion of general-purpose instruction data (replay) into the domain dataset
questions.why: Replaying general data keeps gradients from pulling the model entirely toward the narrow domain, preserving broad skills. More epochs or a higher LR on domain-only data push the weights further from the original model and worsen forgetting.

questions.topic: Choosing a method under tight memory
questions.q: A developer must fine-tune a 13B model on a single 24 GB GPU. Which approach is most practical?
options: Full fine-tuning in BF16
Full fine-tuning in FP32 with gradient accumulation
Training from scratch at 13B
QLoRA (4-bit base model + LoRA adapters)
questions.why: A 13B base in 4-bit is ~6.5 GB, leaving room for small LoRA adapters, their optimizer states and activations. Full fine-tuning would need ~200 GB with Adam; gradient accumulation reduces activation memory per step but not weight, gradient or optimizer memory.

questions.q: A product team needs a model to classify support tickets into 5 categories, has 30 labeled examples, and must ship a prototype this week. What should they try first?
options: Few-shot prompting with a capable instruction-tuned model
Continued pretraining on all ticket history
Full fine-tuning with RLHF
Training a new model from scratch
questions.why: With few labels and a short timeline, prompt engineering with in-context examples is the cheapest baseline and often sufficient; fine-tuning comes later if accuracy or cost requires it. RLHF requires preference data and a complex pipeline and is overkill for a 5-way classifier prototype.

questions.q: Prompting a model with a long system prompt gets the required JSON schema and brand tone right only 80% of the time, and the long prompt adds latency. Which approach best addresses both issues?
options: RAG over the brand guidelines
Increasing sampling temperature
Adding more few-shot examples to the prompt
Supervised fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA) on examples in the required format and tone
questions.why: Fine-tuning bakes consistent style and output structure into the weights, improving reliability and allowing a much shorter prompt. Adding more few-shot examples might help consistency, but it makes the prompt even longer and worsens the latency problem.

questions.q: Which record structure is required to train with DPO (e.g., with TRL's `DPOTrainer`)?
options: `{"text": "..."}` raw documents
`{"prompt": ..., "chosen": ..., "rejected": ...}`
`{"prompt": ..., "completion": ..., "reward": 0.82}`
`{"input": ..., "label": "positive"}`
questions.why: DPO learns from pairwise preferences: for each prompt, a preferred and a dispreferred response. Records with a single completion and a scalar reward fit reward-weighted or RL methods, not the standard pairwise DPO loss.

questions.q: In DPO, what does the hyperparameter β control?
options: The learning rate warmup length
The LoRA rank used for the policy
How strongly the policy is kept close to the reference model (the implicit KL strength)
The ratio of chosen to rejected examples in each batch
questions.why: β plays the role of the KL coefficient in the RLHF objective: higher β keeps the policy closer to the reference, while lower β allows larger deviations to fit the preferences (typical values are around 0.1). It is not a learning-rate or sampling parameter.

questions.q: During PPO, the reward model score keeps rising, but human reviewers find the responses increasingly long, repetitive and sycophantic. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The SFT model was undertrained
The policy is exploiting biases in the reward model (reward hacking), e.g., a preference for length
The KL coefficient is too high
The tokenizer is truncating outputs
questions.why: The reward model is an imperfect proxy; over-optimizing it finds quirks such as length or flattery that score well but do not satisfy humans. A KL coefficient that is too high would keep the policy close to SFT and suppress this drift, so the more likely issue is that it is too low.

questions.q: How many separate networks are typically held in memory during PPO-based RLHF training of an LLM?
options: One: the policy
Two: policy and reward model
Four: policy (actor), value model (critic), frozen reference model, and reward model
Three: policy, reward model and tokenizer model
questions.why: PPO needs the actor and a critic for advantage estimation, the reference for the KL penalty, and the reward model for scores, which makes it memory-hungry. This overhead is a main motivation for DPO (policy + reference only) and critic-free methods.

questions.q: In SFT of a chat model, the loss is commonly computed only on the assistant's response tokens, not the user prompt. Why?
options: It speeds up tokenization
It increases the effective context length
It is required for gradient accumulation to work
The goal is to learn to generate responses, not to model the distribution of user prompts
questions.why: Masking prompt tokens focuses learning on producing good answers and avoids training the model to imitate user messages. The prompt is still processed in the forward pass as context; only its contribution to the loss is excluded.

questions.q:
```python
labels = input_ids.clone()
labels[:, :prompt_len] = -100
loss = model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=labels).loss
```

What is the effect of setting labels to `-100`?
options: Those positions are ignored by the cross-entropy loss
Those tokens are replaced by padding in the input
Those positions receive a large negative reward
Those tokens are masked from attention
questions.why: -100 is PyTorch's default `ignore_index` for `CrossEntropyLoss`, which Hugging Face models use, so these positions contribute nothing to the loss. The input tokens are unchanged and remain visible to attention; labels and attention masks are independent.

questions.q: An SFT dataset has many short examples, and most of each 4,096-token batch is padding. What does sequence packing achieve?
options: It compresses tokens into fewer bits
It removes the need for an attention mask
It truncates long examples to save memory
It concatenates multiple examples into each sequence to reduce wasted padding compute
questions.why: Packing fills each sequence with several examples, greatly improving GPU utilization when samples are short. A correct implementation still needs attention masking or position resets so packed examples do not attend to each other, so the mask is not eliminated.

questions.q: A model fine-tuned with one chat template (special role tokens) gives poor, rambling answers in production. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the GPU supports FP8
Whether the LoRA rank is high enough
Whether the training loss reached zero
Whether inference uses exactly the same chat template and special tokens as training
questions.why: If role markers or end-of-turn tokens differ between training and serving, the model sees out-of-distribution input and may not stop or follow the turn structure. A training loss of zero would indicate memorization, not correct formatting at serving time.

questions.q: On a cluster of 8-GPU DGX nodes connected by InfiniBand, why is tensor parallelism usually limited to the GPUs within one node?
options: Tensor parallelism only works with exactly 8 GPUs
It needs frequent, latency-sensitive collectives in every layer, which suit high-bandwidth NVLink/NVSwitch
InfiniBand does not support all-reduce
Pipeline parallelism cannot be used within a node
questions.why: Tensor parallelism communicates activations several times per layer in both forward and backward passes, so it is placed on the fastest interconnect. Pipeline and data parallelism communicate less often and tolerate slower inter-node links; InfiniBand fully supports NCCL collectives.

questions.q: In pipeline-parallel training, GPUs sit idle at the start and end of each batch (the "bubble"). Which change most directly shrinks the bubble fraction?
options: Splitting each global batch into more micro-batches
Adding more pipeline stages
Disabling gradient accumulation
Using a smaller vocabulary
questions.why: The bubble fraction is roughly (p − 1)/(m + p − 1) for p stages and m micro-batches, so more micro-batches amortize the fill and drain phases. Adding stages increases p, which makes the bubble larger.

questions.q: A team wants to fine-tune with 128K-token sequences, and activations for a single sequence no longer fit on one GPU even with checkpointing. Which parallelism targets this directly?
options: Data parallelism
Context (sequence) parallelism that splits the sequence dimension across GPUs
Expert parallelism
ZeRO stage 1
questions.why: Context parallelism partitions the tokens of a sequence across GPUs and exchanges keys/values for attention, distributing activation memory for very long inputs. Data parallelism splits the batch, so each GPU still has to hold one full long sequence.

questions.q: When training a Mixture-of-Experts model, what does expert parallelism do?
options: Replicates every expert on every GPU
Splits each expert's weight matrices column-wise
Runs experts sequentially on one GPU to save memory
Places different experts on different GPUs and routes tokens to them with all-to-all communication
questions.why: Each GPU hosts a subset of experts; tokens are dispatched to the GPU holding their selected expert and the results are returned, using all-to-all collectives. Splitting an individual expert's matrices is tensor parallelism, which can be combined with expert parallelism.

questions.q: In PyTorch DistributedDataParallel, which collective operation keeps model replicas identical after each backward pass?
options: Broadcast of the loss value
All-to-all of activations
All-reduce of gradients
Gather of optimizer states to rank 0
questions.why: DDP averages gradients across ranks with an all-reduce (overlapped with backward in buckets), so every replica applies the same update. All-to-all is the pattern used for MoE token routing, not gradient synchronization.

questions.q: A job runs on 64 GPUs with tensor-parallel size 8 and pipeline-parallel size 2. What is the data-parallel size?
questions.why: The total GPU count equals TP × PP × DP, so DP = 64 / (8 × 2) = 4 model replicas. 8 would be 64 divided by the TP size alone, ignoring the pipeline dimension.

questions.q:
```python
for i, batch in enumerate(loader):
    loss = model(**batch).loss / accum_steps
    loss.backward()
    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()
```

Why is the loss divided by `accum_steps`?
options: To reduce memory usage of the backward pass
So the summed gradients equal the average over the effective batch, matching large-batch training
To act as a learning-rate warmup
To prevent FP16 underflow
questions.why: `backward()` adds gradients into `.grad`; dividing each micro-batch loss keeps the accumulated gradient an average instead of a sum that grows with `accum_steps`. It has no effect on memory, and it scales values down, which would make FP16 underflow worse rather than better.

questions.q: When using `torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler` with FP16, what must be done before calling `clip_grad_norm_`?
options: Call `scaler.update()`
Call `optimizer.zero_grad()`
Convert the model to FP32
Call `scaler.unscale_(optimizer)` so gradients are clipped at their true magnitude
questions.why: Gradients are still multiplied by the loss scale after backward; clipping them without unscaling would apply the threshold to inflated values. `zero_grad()` before clipping would erase the gradients entirely.

questions.q: With dynamic loss scaling, what happens when `scaler.step(optimizer)` finds inf/NaN values in the gradients?
options: Training stops with an exception
The optimizer step is skipped and the loss scale is reduced
The gradients are clipped to 1.0 and applied
The model is reloaded from the last checkpoint
questions.why: GradScaler skips that update and `scaler.update()` lowers the scale (typically halving it); after a run of clean steps it raises the scale again. Occasional skipped steps are normal, but constant skipping indicates a deeper numerical problem.

questions.q: A training script uses `with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):`. Is a GradScaler normally required?
options: No, BF16's FP32-like exponent range makes gradient underflow rare
Yes, GradScaler is mandatory with any autocast dtype
Yes, because BF16 has more mantissa bits than FP16
No, because autocast converts all gradients to INT8
questions.why: Loss scaling exists to fix FP16's narrow range; BF16 shares FP32's 8-bit exponent, so standard BF16 recipes skip it. BF16 actually has fewer mantissa bits (7) than FP16 (10), so option C has the facts reversed.

questions.q: A run has 50,000 total optimizer steps and the config sets `warmup_ratio=0.02`. How many warmup steps will be used?
questions.why: 0.02 × 50,000 = 1,000 steps of linear LR ramp before the decay schedule begins. 10,000 would correspond to a 20% ratio, a misreading of 0.02 as 0.2.

questions.q: In logit-based knowledge distillation, why is a temperature T > 1 applied to the teacher's and student's softmax?
options: To make the teacher's predictions more confident
To soften distributions so the relative probabilities of non-top classes ("dark knowledge") carry more signal
To speed up the teacher's forward pass
To convert logits into hard labels
questions.why: Dividing logits by T > 1 flattens the distribution, exposing how the teacher ranks alternatives, which is richer than a one-hot label. A higher T makes predictions less confident, not more.

questions.q: A team has only API access to a large teacher LLM (no logits) and wants a small student to imitate it. Which distillation approach is feasible?
options: Matching per-token teacher logits with KL divergence
Copying intermediate hidden states of the teacher
Initializing the student from the teacher's weights
Fine-tuning the student on responses generated by the teacher (sequence-level distillation)
questions.why: With only text outputs, the student can be trained with ordinary SFT on teacher-generated completions. Logit matching and hidden-state matching require white-box access to the teacher's internals. Teacher terms of use should also be checked before distilling.

questions.q: NVIDIA released Nemotron-4 340B with Instruct and Reward models intended for synthetic data pipelines. What is the Reward model's role in such a pipeline?
options: Tokenizing the generated text
Generating the initial prompts
Scoring generated responses so only high-quality samples are kept for training
Serving the final fine-tuned model
questions.why: A typical pipeline generates candidates with an instruct model and uses a reward model (or LLM judge) to score attributes like helpfulness and correctness, filtering out weak samples. Prompt generation is done by the instruct model or templates, not by the reward model.

questions.q: What does the Self-Instruct method do?
options: Lets the model edit its own weights at inference time
Bootstraps an instruction dataset by having an LLM generate new instructions and responses from a small seed set, then filtering them
Trains a reward model without human labels
Replaces SFT with in-context learning
questions.why: Starting from about 175 human-written seed tasks, the model generates new tasks and outputs, which are filtered for quality and diversity and then used for instruction tuning (Alpaca used a variant). It produces SFT data, not reward-model labels.

questions.q: Exact hashing misses documents that differ only by a timestamp or a few words. Which technique is commonly used at scale to find such near-duplicates?
options: MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)
SHA-256 of the full document
Byte-pair encoding
TF-IDF keyword extraction
questions.why: MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity of n-gram sets, and LSH buckets similar signatures so near-duplicates are found without comparing every pair; NeMo Curator implements this on GPUs. A cryptographic hash like SHA-256 changes completely with any edit, so it only catches exact copies.

questions.q: Why do curation pipelines remove text that overlaps with evaluation benchmarks (e.g., by n-gram matching) from training data?
options: Benchmarks contain toxic content
It reduces tokenizer vocabulary size
It shortens training time significantly
Seeing test items during training inflates scores and makes evaluation unreliable
questions.why: If benchmark questions leak into training data, the model can memorize answers, so reported results overstate real capability. The volume removed is tiny, so the purpose is evaluation integrity, not saving compute.

questions.q: A pretraining corpus is 85% web crawl and 15% curated sources (books, code, papers). Teams often sample curated sources more than their raw share. Why?
options: Curated sources tokenize into fewer tokens
Higher-quality sources improve downstream capability per token, so upsampling them helps despite some repetition
Web data cannot be deduplicated
Upsampling eliminates the need for quality filtering
questions.why: Mixture weights are a key pretraining decision; reasoning-dense sources like code and books are often seen for multiple epochs while web text is seen about once. Upsampling complements filtering but does not replace it, because low-quality web data still dominates by volume.

questions.q: LoRA with r = 4 on attention projections plateaus at a high validation loss on a complex code-generation task, while full fine-tuning does much better. What is a sensible next step?
options: Lower the rank to 2 to reduce overfitting
Remove the LoRA dropout
Increase the rank and/or target more modules (e.g., the MLP projections too)
Freeze the LoRA B matrix
questions.why: A plateau far above full fine-tuning suggests the adapter lacks capacity; a larger r and more target modules let it express a richer update. Lowering the rank would further restrict capacity, which is the opposite of what an underfitting adapter needs.

questions.q:
```python
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, "./lora-adapter")
model = model.merge_and_unload()
model.save_pretrained("./merged")
```

What is saved in `./merged`?
options: A standard full model with the LoRA updates folded into the base weights
Only the adapter weights
The base model without any LoRA changes
A 4-bit quantized model
questions.why: `merge_and_unload()` computes W + (α/r)·B·A for each adapted layer and removes the PEFT wrappers, leaving a plain transformers model. Saving the `PeftModel` without merging would write only the small adapter files.

questions.q: What does "double quantization" in QLoRA refer to?
options: Quantizing weights twice, first to 8-bit and then to 4-bit
Quantizing both weights and activations
Quantizing the LoRA adapters as well as the base model
Quantizing the per-block quantization constants themselves to save additional memory
questions.why: Each block of 64 weights has an FP32 scale constant (~0.5 bits/param overhead); double quantization stores these constants in 8-bit, saving about 0.37 bits per parameter. The LoRA adapters stay in BF16 because they are being trained.

questions.q: What problem do QLoRA's paged optimizers address?
options: Slow tokenization of long documents
Out-of-memory errors from transient memory spikes, by paging optimizer states between GPU and CPU memory using unified memory
Divergence caused by large learning rates
Communication overhead in multi-node training
questions.why: Long sequences with gradient checkpointing can cause sudden spikes; NVIDIA unified memory lets optimizer states be evicted to CPU RAM and paged back when needed. Paged optimizers are a single-GPU memory feature and do nothing for multi-node communication.

questions.q:
```python
bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
```

What does `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16` determine?
options: The storage format of the frozen base weights
The dtype of the saved adapter checkpoint
The dtype weights are dequantized to for matrix multiplications
The dtype of the tokenizer's outputs
questions.why: Weights are stored in NF4 (set by `bnb_4bit_quant_type`) but dequantized to the compute dtype, here BF16, for each matmul. Storage format and compute dtype are separate settings, which is why NF4 is described as a storage-only type.

questions.q: Prompt tuning with 20 virtual tokens is applied to a model with hidden size 4,096. How many parameters are trained?
questions.why: Each virtual token is a 4,096-dimensional embedding, so 20 × 4,096 = 81,920 parameters, far fewer than LoRA. 327,680 would correspond to 80 virtual tokens.

questions.q: Lester et al. found that how prompt tuning compares with full fine-tuning depends on model size. What was the finding?
options: Prompt tuning beats full fine-tuning at all model sizes
Prompt tuning only works for models under 1B parameters
Prompt tuning performance is independent of model size
The gap to full fine-tuning shrinks as models grow, becoming small at around 10B+ parameters
questions.why: Soft prompts underperform full fine-tuning on small models, but the gap largely closes at the multi-billion-parameter scale. This is why prompt tuning is most attractive for very large frozen models.

questions.q: Which PEFT method learns small vectors that rescale keys, values and feed-forward activations element-wise, training even fewer parameters than LoRA?
options: Prefix tuning
IA3
Adapter tuning
BitFit
questions.why: IA3 (Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations) multiplies activations by learned vectors, adding only a few parameters per layer. BitFit is also very light, but it trains the existing bias terms instead of adding scaling vectors.

questions.q: A team has a large unlabeled medical corpus and 5,000 medical Q&A pairs, and wants a medical chat assistant. Which ordering is most appropriate?
options: SFT on the Q&A pairs, then continued pretraining on the corpus
DPO first, then continued pretraining
Continued pretraining on the corpus, then SFT on the Q&A pairs (then optional preference alignment)
Only prompt tuning on the corpus
questions.why: Domain knowledge is absorbed first with the next-token objective; SFT then teaches the conversational format on top of that knowledge. Doing continued pretraining after SFT tends to erode the instruction-following behavior SFT just taught.

questions.q: The LIMA study fine-tuned a 65B model on about 1,000 carefully curated examples and got strong results. What is the main lesson?
options: A small, diverse, high-quality SFT set can align response style effectively, since most knowledge comes from pretraining
SFT should always use exactly 1,000 examples
RLHF is required for any instruction-following ability
More data always beats better data in SFT
questions.why: LIMA's "superficial alignment hypothesis" holds that SFT mainly teaches format and style, so curation quality matters more than volume. The 1,000 figure is an illustration, not a rule, and LIMA used no RLHF at all.

questions.q: How is a reward model for RLHF typically built?
options: A separate CNN trained on images of text
A rule-based scorer of keyword matches
A decoder that generates a critique, then a regex extracts a score
A pretrained or SFT transformer with the LM head replaced by a linear head that outputs one scalar
questions.why: The reward model reuses a language model's representations and maps the final token's hidden state to a scalar reward. Generative judges that write critiques exist, but the classic RLHF reward model is a scalar-head classifier-style network.

questions.q: A company has many responses labeled only with thumbs-up or thumbs-down, but no paired comparisons for the same prompt. Which alignment method is designed for this kind of data?
options: KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization)
Standard DPO
Bradley-Terry reward modeling
Prefix tuning
questions.why: KTO learns from unpaired binary desirable/undesirable labels, using a prospect-theory-inspired loss. Standard DPO and Bradley-Terry reward modeling both need chosen/rejected pairs for the same prompt.

questions.q: A reward model r(x, y) is trained on pairs where y_w is preferred over y_l. Which loss is the standard Bradley-Terry formulation?
options: L = −log σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l))
L = −log softmax over the vocabulary of y_w
L = max(0, r(x, y_l) − r(x, y_w))²
questions.why: Bradley-Terry models P(y_w ≻ y_l) = σ(r_w − r_l), so maximizing log-likelihood means minimizing −log σ of the reward margin. Only the difference matters, which makes rewards shift-invariant; the regression option wrongly forces absolute targets of ±1.

questions.q: In DPO, the trained policy π_θ defines an implicit reward. Up to a prompt-dependent constant, what is it?
options: log π_θ(y|x) alone
The reference model's log-probability of y
The length of the response y
β · log(π_θ(y|x) / π_ref(y|x))
questions.why: DPO derives that the optimal KL-regularized policy satisfies r(x, y) = β log(π*/π_ref) + β log Z(x); plugging this into Bradley-Terry cancels Z and gives the DPO loss. Using log π_θ alone would ignore the reference anchor and reduce to a likelihood objective that does not compare the two responses.

questions.q: What does the clipping in PPO's surrogate objective, clip(ρ, 1 − ε, 1 + ε) with ρ = π_θ/π_old, accomplish?
options: It removes the incentive to move the probability ratio beyond about ±ε (e.g., 0.2) in a single update, keeping policy updates conservative
It clips rewards to [−1, 1]
It limits the gradient norm of the value network
It truncates generated responses to a maximum length
questions.why: Taking the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms gives no further gain once the ratio leaves the trust region, which stabilizes training on reused rollouts. Reward clipping and gradient-norm clipping are separate tricks that may be used alongside it.

questions.q: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), used in DeepSeek's reasoning models, differs from PPO mainly in that it:
options: Requires human preference pairs at every step
Drops the learned value model and computes advantages by normalizing rewards within a group of sampled responses to the same prompt
Uses no reward signal at all
Trains only the reward model and freezes the policy
questions.why: GRPO samples several outputs per prompt and uses each output's reward relative to the group mean (divided by the std) as the advantage, removing the critic and its memory cost. It still uses rewards, often verifiable rule-based rewards such as answer correctness for math and code.

questions.q: After a PPO run with KL coefficient β = 0.5, the policy's outputs are nearly identical to the SFT model and reward has barely improved. What is the most likely adjustment?
options: Increase β to 2.0
Remove the reference model and also the reward model
Decrease β so the policy is allowed to move further from the reference
Switch the reward model to a smaller one
questions.why: A KL penalty that is too strong dominates the reward, pinning the policy to the SFT distribution. Raising β would tighten the constraint further, while lowering it too much risks reward hacking, so β is tuned while monitoring KL and human or gold-model quality.

questions.q: Transformer Engine's common "hybrid" FP8 recipe uses which formats?
options: E5M2 for forward activations and weights, E4M3 for gradients
E4M3 for forward activations and weights, E5M2 for gradients
E8M0 for all tensors
INT8 for weights and FP8 E5M2 for activations
questions.why: E4M3 has more precision (max ~448), which suits forward tensors; E5M2 has more dynamic range (max ~57,344), which suits gradients. Option A swaps the two, which is the most common confusion.

questions.q: In Transformer Engine's delayed scaling recipe, how is the scale factor for an FP8 tensor chosen?
options: It is fixed at 1.0 for all tensors
It is set manually by the user per layer
It is computed from the current tensor's exact maximum before every cast
It is derived from a history of absolute-maximum (amax) values recorded in previous iterations
questions.why: Delayed scaling keeps an amax history window and computes the next scale from it, avoiding an extra pass over each tensor before casting. Computing the exact current maximum (just-in-time or "current" scaling) is more accurate but costs an additional reduction per tensor.

questions.q: In mixed-precision Adam training, about 16 bytes per parameter are needed. Which components make up 12 of those bytes?
options: FP32 master weights, FP32 first moment (m), and FP32 second moment (v)
BF16 weights, BF16 gradients and FP32 master weights
FP32 gradients, FP32 activations and BF16 weights
FP32 weights, FP32 gradients and the KV cache
questions.why: The full breakdown is 2 (BF16/FP16 weights) + 2 (16-bit gradients) + 4 (FP32 master) + 4 (m) + 4 (v) = 16 bytes; the 12 FP32 optimizer bytes are what ZeRO stage 1 shards. Activations are excluded from the rule of thumb, and a KV cache is an inference structure.

questions.q: A 70B model is fully sharded with ZeRO stage 3 across 64 GPUs. Using 16 bytes/param and ignoring activations and temporary buffers, how much model-state memory does each GPU hold?
options: 140 GB
70 GB
2.2 GB
questions.why: Total model state is 70B × 16 B = 1,120 GB; sharding everything across 64 GPUs gives 1,120 / 64 = 17.5 GB each. 140 GB is just the BF16 weights unsharded, which is what each GPU would hold for weights alone under plain data parallelism.

questions.q: Compared with standard data parallelism (all-reduce of gradients), roughly how does ZeRO stage 3 change per-step communication volume?
options: It eliminates communication entirely
It halves communication volume
It increases it to about 1.5×, due to all-gathering parameters in forward and backward plus reduce-scattering gradients
It increases it 64× on 64 GPUs
questions.why: An all-reduce costs about 2Ψ per GPU; ZeRO-3 adds parameter all-gathers (Ψ in forward and Ψ in backward) plus a reduce-scatter (Ψ), about 3Ψ, i.e., 1.5×. Communication per GPU does not grow linearly with GPU count, so 64× is wrong.

questions.q: With a GPipe/1F1B-style schedule, 4 pipeline stages and 12 micro-batches per step, what fraction of time is approximately lost to the pipeline bubble, using (p − 1)/(m + p − 1)?
questions.why: (4 − 1)/(12 + 4 − 1) = 3/15 = 20%. Using (p − 1)/m = 3/12 gives 25%, the ratio of bubble time to ideal compute time rather than the fraction of total time.

questions.q: Megatron-LM's interleaved 1F1B schedule assigns each GPU several non-contiguous chunks of layers (virtual stages). What is the trade-off?
options: Lower memory but more pipeline bubble
A smaller pipeline bubble but more point-to-point communication
No bubble at all and no extra communication
Higher accuracy but slower convergence
questions.why: With v model chunks per device, the bubble shrinks by about a factor of v, but activations cross device boundaries v times more often. The schedule changes only how work is scheduled, so it does not affect model accuracy.

questions.q: In Megatron-style tensor parallelism of a transformer MLP (Y = GeLU(X·A)·B), A is split by columns and B by rows. Why this combination?
options: The nonlinearity can be applied locally to each partition, so the forward pass needs only one all-reduce at the end of the MLP
It allows each GPU to hold the entire weight matrix
It avoids any communication in the backward pass
It makes the MLP compatible with pipeline parallelism only
questions.why: Column-splitting A gives each GPU a full slice of hidden units, so GeLU needs no synchronization; row-splitting B produces partial sums that one all-reduce combines. The backward pass still needs a matching all-reduce on the input gradients.

questions.q: In Megatron-LM, "sequence parallelism" (used together with tensor parallelism) does what?
options: Splits the batch dimension across nodes
Replaces attention with a linear-time approximation
Splits attention heads across pipeline stages
Partitions LayerNorm and dropout activations along the sequence dimension in regions that tensor parallelism would otherwise replicate
questions.why: Outside the TP-split attention and MLP blocks, activations are duplicated on each TP rank; sequence parallelism shards them by token and replaces the all-reduce with reduce-scatter/all-gather at the same communication volume. Attention itself remains exact, so no approximation is involved.

questions.q: How does ring-attention-style context parallelism compute exact attention over a sequence split across N GPUs?
options: Each GPU attends only to its local chunk, ignoring other tokens
Key/value blocks are passed around a ring of GPUs, and each GPU accumulates attention for its queries with online softmax while overlapping communication with compute
The full sequence is gathered on GPU 0 for attention
Attention is approximated with random features
questions.why: After N − 1 exchanges every query block has seen every key/value block, so the result is exact, and no GPU ever holds the full sequence's K/V at once. Local-only attention would change the model's outputs, so it is not exact attention.

questions.q: In a bandwidth-optimal ring all-reduce of a gradient buffer of size S across N GPUs, how much data does each GPU send?
options: S × N
S / N
S × log₂N
questions.why: A ring all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, each moving (N − 1)/N × S per GPU, so the per-GPU volume stays nearly constant (~2S) as N grows. S × log₂N describes tree-based algorithms' step count, not the ring's bandwidth cost.

questions.q: Megatron-LM's *selective* activation recomputation differs from full checkpointing by:
options: Recomputing every layer twice
Recomputing only the attention parts whose activations are large but cheap to recompute (e.g., softmax and dropout outputs)
Offloading all activations to NVMe
Storing activations in FP8 instead of recomputing
questions.why: Attention score tensors grow with sequence length squared but require few FLOPs to regenerate, so recomputing only them saves most of the memory at a small compute overhead. Full checkpointing recomputes whole layers, which costs much more compute.

questions.q: A pretraining team wants to be able to extend a run with more tokens later without restarting, which is awkward when cosine decay is tied to a fixed total step count. Which learning-rate schedule is designed for this?
options: A constant learning rate with no decay at all
Cosine decay with a longer warmup
Step decay at the end of every epoch
Warmup-Stable-Decay: hold a constant LR, then run a short decay phase whenever a final checkpoint is needed
questions.why: WSD keeps the LR flat for most of training, so the run can be continued from any stable-phase checkpoint, and a brief cooldown produces a strong model on demand. A constant LR with no decay phase usually leaves the loss noticeably higher than a decayed schedule.

questions.q: PaLM added an auxiliary "z-loss" of about 1e-4 · log²Z, where Z is the softmax normalizer over the vocabulary. What is its purpose?
options: To keep output logits from drifting to large magnitudes, improving numerical stability
To encourage diverse token predictions
To balance load across experts
To penalize long responses
questions.why: Pushing log Z toward 0 keeps the softmax normalizer well-conditioned, which reduces instabilities, especially in low precision. Expert load balancing uses a different auxiliary loss that operates on router probabilities, not output logits.

questions.q: Why do Mixture-of-Experts training recipes add an auxiliary load-balancing loss on the router?
options: To reduce the number of total parameters
To prevent routing collapse, where a few experts receive most tokens while others are undertrained and capacity overflows
To make all experts learn identical functions
To remove the need for expert parallelism
questions.why: The auxiliary loss rewards a uniform distribution of tokens across experts, keeping all experts utilized and GPU loads balanced. It balances how much each expert is used without making experts identical; specialization is the point of MoE.

questions.q: Using the approximation C ≈ 6·N·D FLOPs, how much compute does it take to train a 7B-parameter model on 2 trillion tokens?
options: About 1.4 × 10²²
About 2.8 × 10²²
About 8.4 × 10²²
About 8.4 × 10²⁴
questions.why: 6 × 7×10⁹ × 2×10¹² = 8.4 × 10²² FLOPs (2ND for the forward pass, 4ND for the backward pass). 2.8 × 10²² uses 2ND, which counts only the forward pass.

questions.q: Training a 7B model, each H100 processes 10,000 tokens/s. Using 6N FLOPs per token and a dense BF16 peak of ~989 TFLOPS, what is the approximate MFU?
options: About 7%
About 21%
About 85%
About 42%
questions.why: Achieved = 6 × 7×10⁹ × 10⁴ = 4.2 × 10¹⁴ FLOP/s = 420 TFLOPS; 420 / 989 ≈ 42%. 21% results from using 3N instead of 6N per token; MFU of 35–55% is typical for well-tuned large-scale runs.

questions.q: The QLoRA paper's experiments on target modules found that matching full fine-tuning quality required what?
options: Applying LoRA to all linear layers of the transformer blocks, not just query and value projections
Applying LoRA only to the embedding layer
Using rank r ≥ 256
Applying LoRA only to the final layer
questions.why: The QLoRA authors reported that adapter placement across all linear layers mattered more than rank, which was a relatively insensitive hyperparameter. This is why many recipes now target q, k, v, o and the MLP projections.

questions.q: What does DoRA (Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) change compared with LoRA?
options: It removes the B matrix and trains only A
It decomposes each weight into magnitude and direction, training the magnitude vector directly and applying a LoRA update to the direction
It quantizes adapters to 2 bits
It applies LoRA to the optimizer states
questions.why: Separating magnitude from direction makes DoRA's learning dynamics closer to full fine-tuning, often improving accuracy at the same rank. Like LoRA, it can be merged into the weights after training.

questions.q: Rank-stabilized LoRA (rsLoRA) argues the standard α/r scaling makes high-rank adapters learn too slowly. What scaling does it use instead?
options: α · r
α / r²
1 (no scaling)
α / √r
questions.why: With α/r, the update's magnitude shrinks as rank grows, so larger ranks bring little gain; α/√r keeps learning stable and lets higher ranks improve results. In HF PEFT this is enabled with `use_rslora=True`.

questions.topic: Why LoRA steps aren't much faster
questions.q: LoRA trains <1% of parameters, yet each training step is only modestly faster than full fine-tuning. Why?
options: LoRA adapters are computed on the CPU
LoRA requires twice as many optimizer steps
The forward pass and backpropagation of activation gradients still go through the entire frozen model
LoRA disables mixed precision
questions.why: To reach adapters in early layers, gradients must flow back through every layer; LoRA saves only frozen-weight gradient computation, optimizer updates, and memory. Its main win is memory and storage, not a large per-step speedup (the LoRA paper reported ~25% higher throughput on GPT-3).

questions.q: When merging several fine-tuned models built from the same base, TIES-merging differs from simply averaging their task vectors by:
options: Trimming small parameter changes, resolving sign conflicts by majority, and merging only agreeing values
Retraining the merged model from scratch
Concatenating the models as experts in a MoE
Selecting the single best model's weights
questions.why: Naive averaging lets redundant tiny updates and opposite-sign updates cancel useful changes; TIES (Trim, Elect Sign, Merge) reduces this interference. Merging requires no additional training, unlike retraining or distillation.

questions.q: NEFTune reported improved instruction-tuned chat quality with a one-line change during SFT. What is that change?
options: Adding dropout to the LM head
Adding random noise to the input embedding vectors during training
Shuffling tokens within each example
Doubling the learning rate after warmup
questions.why: NEFTune adds scaled uniform noise to embeddings during fine-tuning only, acting as a regularizer that reduces overfitting to the instruction set's specifics. Shuffling tokens would destroy the meaning of the training text rather than regularize it.

questions.q: In Hinton-style distillation, the soft-target KL term is multiplied by T². Why?
