options: To make the teacher's logits larger
To convert KL divergence into cross-entropy
To normalize by vocabulary size
Gradients of the softened term scale as 1/T², so multiplying by T² keeps its magnitude comparable to the hard-label loss
questions.why: Without the correction, raising T would silently shrink the soft-target term's contribution, entangling the temperature with the loss weighting. KL and cross-entropy differ only by the teacher-entropy constant, so T² plays no role in converting between them.

questions.topic: Forward vs reverse KL in distillation
questions.q: Methods like MiniLLM distill generative LLMs by minimizing *reverse* KL, KL(student ‖ teacher), on student-sampled outputs. Why?
options: Reverse KL is mode-seeking, so a small student concentrates on the teacher's high-probability modes instead of spreading mass over regions it cannot model well
Reverse KL needs no teacher at all
Reverse KL is identical to forward KL for language models
Reverse KL removes the need for sampling
questions.why: Forward KL is mass-covering, pushing a low-capacity student to assign probability everywhere the teacher does, which can produce low-quality generations. Reverse KL requires samples from the student, so it relies on on-policy sampling rather than removing it.

questions.q: How does Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) reduce catastrophic forgetting?
options: By freezing all layers except the last
By adding a quadratic penalty that discourages changing parameters with high Fisher information for previous tasks
By replaying old training data
By distilling from a larger model
questions.why: EWC estimates each parameter's importance to earlier tasks (diagonal Fisher) and anchors important weights near their old values. It is a regularization approach that needs no old data, unlike replay.

questions.q: When continued pretraining starts from a fully decayed checkpoint with a new LR warmup, the loss on the original pretraining distribution rises at first. What combination do studies recommend to get domain gains while limiting this?
options: Keep the LR at the old minimum and train only on new data
Reset the optimizer and use a 10× higher peak LR
Re-warm and re-decay the learning rate, and replay a small fraction of the original pretraining data
Freeze all attention layers
questions.why: Re-warming is needed to learn the new distribution efficiently but causes some forgetting; mixing in even a few percent of old data mitigates it (Ibrahim et al., 2024). Staying at the tiny final LR limits forgetting but also learns the new domain poorly.

questions.q: An engineer adds 500 new special tokens to the tokenizer, calls `model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))`, then trains LoRA on attention projections only. The model never uses the new tokens sensibly. What was missed?
options: The LoRA rank was too high
Gradient checkpointing was not enabled
The tokenizer must be retrained from scratch
The new embedding rows (and LM head) were never trained; they should be made trainable, e.g., via `modules_to_save=["embed_tokens", "lm_head"]`
questions.why: Resizing initializes new embedding rows that stay frozen under attention-only LoRA, so the model cannot learn to represent or emit the new tokens. Retraining the whole tokenizer is unnecessary; the newly added rows simply need to be trainable.

questions.q: An SFT trainer averages the per-token loss within each micro-batch and then averages across accumulation steps. Micro-batches have very different numbers of non-padded response tokens. What is the effect?
options: Tokens in short micro-batches get more weight than tokens in long ones, so results differ from true large-batch training
No effect; the result equals the token-level mean over the full batch
Gradients become zero for padded micro-batches
The learning rate is effectively doubled
questions.why: A mean of means equals the global token mean only when every micro-batch has the same token count; the correct approach sums token losses and divides by the total token count across all accumulated micro-batches. This bug was found and fixed in popular trainers in 2024.

questions.q: A team quadruples the global batch size (scaling the LR accordingly) but sees almost no reduction in optimizer steps needed to reach a target loss. What explains this?
options: Gradient accumulation was used, which invalidates large batches
The batch is beyond the critical batch size, where more samples per step mainly reduce gradient noise that is no longer the bottleneck
Larger batches always need more steps
The learning-rate warmup was too long
questions.why: Below the critical batch size, doubling the batch nearly halves the steps needed; above it, returns diminish and the extra compute is largely wasted. Gradient accumulation produces mathematically equivalent large batches, so it is not the cause.

questions.q: Gao et al. studied optimizing a policy against a proxy reward model while measuring a larger "gold" reward model. As KL divergence from the initial policy grows, what happens to the gold score?
options: It rises monotonically with the proxy score
It stays constant
It falls immediately from the first step
It rises at first, then peaks and declines even while the proxy score keeps rising
questions.why: This is Goodhart's law in RLHF: past a point, the policy exploits proxy errors, and true quality drops. Larger reward models and KL control shift the peak but do not remove it, which is why early stopping and monitoring are needed.

questions.q: Llama 2-Chat used "rejection sampling" fine-tuning in addition to PPO. What does it involve?
options: Sampling K responses per prompt, selecting the highest-reward one with the reward model, and fine-tuning on these best samples
Rejecting all prompts the model answers incorrectly from the dataset
Filtering pretraining data with a toxicity classifier
Discarding gradients that exceed a norm threshold
questions.why: Best-of-K selection followed by SFT on the winners is a simple, stable way to improve a policy with a reward model, closely related to expert iteration. Discarding large gradients describes gradient clipping or skipping, which has nothing to do with this method.

questions.q: A lab trains each new model generation mostly on text generated by the previous generation, with little fresh human data. What long-term effect has research (e.g., Shumailov et al.) shown?
options: Continual improvement without limit
Faster convergence with no quality change
Model collapse: rare "tail" content disappears and outputs become increasingly homogeneous and distorted
Improved calibration on rare events
questions.why: Each generation slightly under-samples low-probability content, and these errors compound recursively until the learned distribution narrows. Keeping a share of real data and filtering synthetic data carefully mitigates this, so synthetic data is useful as a supplement but not as a full replacement.
